tasks: wscript never allocates a console; heartbeat still needs one admin run (DEVLOG #40b)

The user confirmed the flash still happened after DEVLOG #40, and it was
never really fixed: -WindowStyle Hidden is a request PowerShell applies
after it starts, and Windows can allocate a console in the instant
before that regardless of Settings.Hidden. wscript.exe running
ops/run_hidden.vbs (WScript.Shell.Run ..., 0, False) never allocates one
at all - the standard, decades-old fix for exactly this.

Own mistake along the way: attempting this non-elevated, an
Unregister-ScheduledTask on theta-desk-watchdog succeeded and the
re-register failed for real (Access is denied, not the false-positive
kind from #40) - the task briefly did not exist. Restored it immediately
via a plain (non-S4U) registration; same safe path applied to keepalive,
low-stakes. heartbeat - the actual trading tick - was left untouched
rather than risk the same failure on it: switching an Action's
executable genuinely needs elevation, unlike the argument-only change
in #40.

ops/harden_task.ps1 rewritten to do all five tasks in one elevated pass:
wscript launcher plus S4U restored wherever this session had to drop it.
ops/hide_windows.ps1 removed, superseded.

g6: a leg fails only if it is wide BOTH ways (DEVLOG #36c)

Per cent alone is the wrong instrument for a cheap contract. A wing
quoted 0.15/0.20 is '28.6% wide' and costs $3 a contract to cross; a
$5.00 contract at 9.5% costs $50. The relative cap refused the first and
passed the second.

Measured: on Sep 3 the gate refused ten candidates whose widest leg cost
between one and three dollars to cross, and 206 of the 282 contracts it
rejected chain-wide were penny-wide. Both of today's open-session ticks
refused on the same gate (QQQ 743C at 9.8%, QQQ 753C at 13.6%) — legs
whose absolute spread is three cents.

A leg now fails only when it is over the relative cap AND over an
absolute one ($0.10 a share). Everything genuinely expensive to cross
still fails; the absolute test is an escape for cheapness, never for
width. max_abs_spread: 0.0 restores the pure relative cap. The hedge's
own liquidity check gets the same treatment — a 5-delta put is the
cheapest contract in the book and exactly the case per cent reads wrong.

a quiet pass writes nothing; the watchdog watches the fast loop (DEVLOG #36b)

Reviewed yesterday's work as a stranger and the worst thing in it was
mine. A pass journalled three lines a minute: 364 passes a session is
1,092 lines against 1,177 for the desk's entire first week, and the
console's 900-row blotter would have been evicted of every decision the
desk ever made. Plus 1,456 mark rows a session across four books against
357 in total today. The feature that demonstrates discipline would have
buried the mechanism that proves it.

The journal is the decision record, not a process pulse. A tick always
opens its record — fifteen minutes is a decision whether or not it
traded. A pass opens one lazily: the first real event writes
manage_start ahead of itself, and a pass with no events writes nothing.
Integrity is recorded by a tick every time and by a pass only when the
verdict CHANGED; the alerts already fire on the transition. Marks run on
a cadence (manage.mark_every_passes, ~5 min) and always when the pass
acted, so a close lands on the curve the minute it fires.

That a pass RAN is a fact about the process, not a decision: it lives in
the store as last_manage_ts plus manage_passes / manage_closes counters,
which is where the watchdog and the console now read it.

Second hole, same pass of the eye: the watchdog only knew about ticks. If
the loop died at 14:00, exits would fall back to fifteen minutes and
nothing would say so — the desk looks healthy with its fast hand gone. It
gets its own marker and its own page (WARN, not CRITICAL: positions are
still managed, just slower). Preflight checks the last pass's age, but
only while the exchange is open — a shut exchange puts the loop to sleep,
so an old stamp overnight is the design.

manager: a timed-out pass releases its own lock; the loop outlives any pass

A pass killed on timeout never reaches its finally, and its tick_lock
would sit until the 10-minute stale limit — a quarter hour in which the
tick skips and every pass yields. The lock's value is the instant it was
taken; one taken after the pass started is the pass's own and is cleared.
Any other failure to run a pass is logged and the loop goes on.

size ladder + one-minute management pass (DEVLOG #36)

Why the number was small, measured: +$598 on $3,165 of closed risk is
+18.9% on the risk actually taken — better than the leader's +16.2% on
equity at 35% of the book. The desk was not behind on decisions; it was

risks ~$830 for one contract, so a second never fit. Nine structures, nine

engine/ladder.py — every ceiling is a rung, not a constant. Earned by
closed core trades with a non-negative realised result (0 / 5 / 15 ->
2 / 3 / 4% per structure, 5 / 8 / 10% new risk a day, 10 / 15 / 18% book
cap), taken back by drawdown at 2% (one rung) and 3.5% (all), below the
4% halt. The table is validated on load: no rung below the risk.* floor,
no fraction ever steps down. `ladder.enabled: false` is the desk exactly
as it traded through Sep 3 — that is the rollback. The tick journals the
rung as `ladder` before it sizes; `gates` carries it too. Today's record
resolves to establish: the same condor goes out at three lots.

Found when qty stopped being one: release_new_risk gave the daily budget
back one lot for an n-lot order (the row's max_loss is per unit; the
charge was unit x qty). Same class in the export, where the console
would have compared a third of the real worst case to the ceiling, and
in the fill alert. Fixed in all three, plus the partial-fill path; the
reality check now sums max_loss x qty and climbs the ladder by hand.

thetadesk.main manage + tools/manager.py + ops/manager.ps1 — the tick
decides every fifteen minutes; a pass every minute manages what it
decided: reconcile, integrity, re-mark, exits, closes. It cannot open
anything (cmd_tick returns before the selector). Same lock as the tick;
a tick that lands on a pass now waits up to a minute instead of
skipping a quarter hour. Holds are not journaled and spend no snapshot;
a pass that produces an order writes its snapshot first, so it replays
exactly like a tick. Marks every minute. Windowless via pythonw, in
Startup, steps aside in the scheduler's minutes, sleeps while shut.

research: teardown of trdrbot, Convexity and Uncharted

Three repositories cloned and read, three live boards read, plus the
scoreboard and trade ledger. research/TEARDOWN.md records what each one
actually does and — the point of the exercise — why our number is small.

The answer is not strategy quality. Realised +$598 on $3,165 of closed
risk is +18.9% on the risk actually taken. trdrbot's +16.2% is on equity
while carrying 35% of the book at risk and $81,868 of beta-weighted
delta; their own scorecard puts their Brier at 0.225 against 0.25 for a
coin and files 8 of 13 closed positions under "luck".

We are not behind on decisions. We are behind on size.

Measured: every structure was opened at qty 1. The per-structure ceiling
of 1.25% is the binding constraint — a $10-wide iron condor costs ~$830
for one contract, 66% of the ceiling, so a second contract never fits.
The daily budget ran at 93%. The book ceiling never bound at all: 21%.
Cumulative risk deployed all week was 4.85% of equity.

For scale: trdrbot's lowest tier, day one, no history, is 5% per
position and 10% per book. Uncharted's published doctrine is 3% per
position. Ours is the tightest of the four by a factor of three.

Also recorded: Convexity's full RiskGate table, their 15-second
reduce-only loop, and their own post-mortem — a day where every single
trade was legal and the book still lost, because every open position was
the same short call spread. Gates that check trades cannot see a book.
Our g8 reprices the whole book and is stronger than theirs; that should
be said out loud rather than left implicit.
